pages.c10-p01: Explain object-oriented programming terminology: class, object, attribute (property), method (behaviour), constructor and instantiation
pages.c10-p02: Explain the purpose of a method's parameter list and return type
pages.c10-p03: Explain encapsulation and its benefits, including private attributes accessed through get and set methods
pages.c10-p04: Write classes in C#, create objects from them and predict the output of object-oriented code
pages.c10-p05: Represent a class using a class diagram, including visibility symbols
pages.c10-p06: Explain inheritance using the terms superclass (base class) and subclass (derived class), and represent a class hierarchy in a diagram
pages.c10-p07: Write C# subclasses that inherit from a base class, call the base constructor and add their own attributes and methods
pages.c10-p08: Explain polymorphism and implement it by overriding methods (virtual, abstract and override)
pages.c10-p09: Evaluate the object-oriented approach, discussing its advantages and disadvantages
pages.c10-p10: Describe event-driven programming and the use of events, event handlers and controls in a graphical user interface

q.q: Which statement best describes an object?
o: A template that defines the attributes and methods of a type
A specific instance of a class with its own attribute values
A special method that runs automatically when a class is created
A data item declared in a class that every instance shares
q.why: The class is the template; the object is an instance of it with its own values.

q.q: What is a class?
o: One specific instance holding its own values for the attributes it was given
A subroutine describing what an object can do or what can be done to it
A template defining the attributes and methods every object of that type will have
The values held in an object's attributes at a particular moment in time
q.why: A class is a blueprint; the other options describe an object, a method and state.

q.q: What happens when new LibraryBook("00123", "Maths") runs?
o: The Describe method is called on every LibraryBook
Every existing LibraryBook object is updated
The LibraryBook class is compiled for the first time
An object is instantiated and the constructor runs
q.why: new creates an object and calls the constructor to give it a sensible starting state.

q.q: How can you recognise a constructor in C#?
o: It has the class's name and returns void
It is always declared private in the class
It is always called Main and has no parameters
It has the class's name and no return type
q.why: A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type, not even void.

q.q: In the LibraryBook class, onLoan is declared as private bool onLoan;. What is it?
o: An attribute
A method
An object
A constructor
q.why: It is a data item declared in the class; each object has its own value.

q.q: In the LibraryBook class, Lend() sets onLoan to true. What is Lend()?
o: An attribute
A method
A constructor
A class
q.why: Methods (behaviours) are subroutines in the class describing what an object can do or what can be done to it.

q.q: What is the term for the values held in an object's attributes at a given moment?
o: Its state
Its class
Its instantiation
Its interface
q.why: The values held in an object's attributes at a given moment are its state.

q.q: b1 and b2 are both LibraryBook objects. b1.Lend(); is called. What happens to b2?
o: b2 is also marked as on loan
b2 is deleted and recreated
b2 now refers to the same book as b1
Nothing; only b1's state changes
q.why: Each object holds its own attribute values, so a method call changes only the object it is called on.

q.q: How does object-oriented programming differ from procedural programming?
o: Objects bundle data with the code that acts on it; procedural data sits in separate variables
Procedural programs bundle data with code; OOP keeps data in separate variables
OOP programs never use subroutines, whereas procedural programs always do
OOP programs cannot use selection or iteration, only method calls
q.why: In OOP each object bundles its data with its methods; in a procedural program data is passed into free-standing procedures and functions.

q.q: In C#, how is a method called on the object referred to by b1?
o: With square brackets, as in b1[Lend]
With the new keyword, as in new b1.Lend()
With an arrow, as in b1->Lend()
With dot notation, as in b1.Lend()
q.why: Methods are called with dot notation on the variable that holds a reference to the object.

q.q: What does an empty parameter list () in a method header tell you?
o: The method returns nothing to the caller
The method needs no extra information when called
The method is private to its own class
The method is the class's constructor
q.why: No parameters means no arguments are passed. Returning nothing is shown by void.

q.q: Which header is most likely to be a set method?
o: public void SetAge(int newAge)
public int SetAge()
public void GetAge(int age)
public int GetAge()
q.why: A setter takes the new value as a parameter and returns nothing.

q.q: A method has the return type double. What must it contain?
o: A return statement that supplies a double
A parameter of type double in its header
A Console.WriteLine to show the double
The keyword void before its name
q.why: A non-void method must return a value of its declared type.

q.q: In the header public bool Buy(double price), what is bool?
o: The access modifier
The return type
The parameter list
The method name
q.why: The four parts are access modifier (public), return type (bool), name (Buy) and parameter list (double price).

q.q: What does the return type void mean?
o: The method needs no parameters when it is called
The method carries out an action and returns nothing
The method can only be called from inside its class
The method returns a value of any type it chooses
q.why: void means nothing is sent back; an empty parameter list means no parameters are needed.

q.q: Buy is declared public bool Buy(double price). Why will acc.Buy("chips") not compile?
o: Buy returns a bool, so its result must always be stored in a variable
The argument must match the parameter's type, and "chips" is not a double
Methods with a return type cannot be given any arguments when called
A string argument must be passed by reference using the ref keyword
q.why: Arguments must match the parameters in number, order and type.

q.q: An account's balance starts at 0. acc.TopUp(10.00); then bool ok = acc.Buy(3.20); runs. What are ok and the balance?
o: true and 10
false and 6.8
true and 6.8
false and 10
q.why: 3.20 is not more than the balance of 10, so Buy subtracts it and returns true, leaving 6.8.

q.q: The balance is 6.8. What is output by Console.WriteLine(acc.Buy(50.00));?
o: True
False
q.why: 50 is more than the balance, so Buy returns false without changing it. C# prints a bool as False with a capital letter.

q.q: What is the usual pattern for a getter?
o: One parameter and a void return type
One parameter and a return type of bool
An empty parameter list and a return type matching the attribute
An empty parameter list and a void return type
q.why: A getter needs no input and returns the attribute's type; a setter normally has one parameter and returns void.

q.q: TopUp is written as public void TopUp(double amount) { if (amount > 0) balance += amount; }. What does acc.TopUp(-5) do?
o: It reduces the balance by 5
Nothing; the balance is unchanged
It causes a compile-time error
It returns false to the caller
q.why: The condition amount > 0 is false, so no change is made; a void method returns nothing.

q.q: Which is the best definition of encapsulation?
o: Creating a new class that takes on the attributes and methods of an existing class
Allowing objects of different classes to respond to the same call in their own way
Creating an object from a class by calling its constructor with the new keyword
Combining data and methods in a class, with the data hidden and accessed only through methods
q.why: Encapsulation has three parts: data and methods in one class, private attributes, access through get/set methods. The others are inheritance, polymorphism and instantiation.

q.q: How is an attribute made read-only in an encapsulated class?
o: Declare the attribute public instead of private
Provide a set method but no get method
Give the attribute no data type at all
Provide a get method but no set method
q.why: Without a setter, nothing outside the class can change it.

q.q: Why are attributes declared private?
o: So that subclasses can change them freely
Because C# will not compile public attributes
So that the program runs more quickly
So they can only be accessed through the class's methods
q.why: Private hides the data so access is controlled by methods.

q.q: Which is a benefit of using a set method rather than a public attribute?
o: It removes the need for a constructor in the class
The new value can be validated before it is stored
It makes the attribute read-only from outside
It means the attribute uses less memory
q.why: The setter can reject invalid values, protecting the object's state.

q.q: A Patient object has weight 62.5. p.SetWeight(-4); then p.SetWeight(60.8); run, where SetWeight only accepts values above 0 and below 400. What is the weight now?
q.why: -4 is refused by the validation, then 60.8 is accepted.

q.q: The Patient class has GetHospitalNo() but no SetHospitalNo(). What does this achieve?
o: The hospital number can be changed only by subclasses
The hospital number is hidden even from the getter
The hospital number cannot be changed after the object is created
The hospital number must be set again on each use
q.why: A getter without a setter makes an attribute read-only.

q.q: The Patient class is changed to store weight in grams internally, but GetWeight() still returns kilograms. Which benefit of encapsulation does this show?
o: Easier maintenance: callers depend only on the public methods
Data integrity: invalid weights are always refused
Read-only data: the weight can no longer be changed
Related actions: the date of each weigh-in is logged
q.why: Because other code uses only public methods, the internal storage can be redesigned without breaking it.

q.q: In the C# property set { if (value > 0) weightKg = value; }, what is value?
o: The current value of weightKg before the change
A constant defined elsewhere in the class
The value returned by the get accessor
The new value being assigned to the property
q.why: In a property's set accessor, value holds the new value being assigned.

q.q: Why can no code outside the Patient class write weightKg = 0;?
o: weightKg is protected, so only subclasses of Patient can use it
weightKg is a constant, so its value can never be changed at all
weightKg has no getter, so it cannot be named outside the class
weightKg is private, so only code inside Patient can use it directly
q.why: Private members are hidden from other code, which reduces accidental errors.

q.q: A set method also records the date each time a weight changes. Which benefit of encapsulation is this?
o: The internal storage can be redesigned without breaking calling code
The attribute becomes read-only once the object has been created
Related actions are kept together, so callers do not have to remember them
The object runs faster because the date is calculated only once
q.why: A setter can carry out side effects such as logging, so callers need not remember to do it.

q.q: What does this.owner = owner; do in the Locker constructor?
o: Copies the parameter into the object's owner attribute
Copies the object's owner attribute into the parameter
Compares the parameter with the owner attribute
Creates a new Locker object called owner
q.why: this.owner is the attribute; owner on the right is the parameter with the same name.

q.q: Locker a is created for Niamh. After a.Lock(); a.ChangeOwner("Jack"); what is a's owner?
o: Jack
Niamh
Callum
null
q.why: ChangeOwner only works when the locker is not locked, so the change is silently refused.

q.q: Why has the Locker class no SetNumber method?
o: The locker number should never change after the object is created
Setters must always be declared private in C#
The constructor is not able to set the locker number
C# does not allow set methods for int attributes
q.why: Leaving out the setter makes the number read-only.

q.q: Locker b is created as new Locker(27, "Callum") and b.ChangeOwner("Erin"); runs. What does b.Status() return?
o: Locker 27 (Callum): open
Locker 27 (Erin): locked
Locker 27 (Callum): locked
Locker 27 (Erin): open
q.why: b is never locked, so the change of owner succeeds and the state is open.

q.q: Locker a (14, Niamh) is locked, ChangeOwner("Jack") is refused, then a.Unlock(); a.ChangeOwner("Jack"); run. What does a.Status() return?
o: Locker 14 (Niamh): open
Locker 14 (Jack): locked
Locker 14 (Jack): open
Locker 14 (Niamh): locked
q.why: After unlocking, the second ChangeOwner succeeds, and isLocked is false.

q.q: A programmer writes public void Locker(int number, string owner) instead of a constructor. What is the effect?
o: It still runs as a constructor, but it can no longer return a value
The compiler adds the missing return statement automatically
Objects can no longer be created from the Locker class at all
It becomes an ordinary method, and objects are built with default values
q.why: Giving a constructor a return type turns it into an ordinary method, so the object gets default values.

q.q: In the Locker class, what does isLocked ? "locked" : "open" do?
o: Sets isLocked to true and returns "locked"
Asks the user whether the locker is locked
Chooses "locked" if isLocked is true, otherwise "open"
Chooses "open" if isLocked is true, otherwise "locked"
q.why: The ? : operator picks the first value when the condition is true and the second when it is false.

q.q: Which is the correct order of parts when writing a class, as recommended in the notes?
o: Constructor, getters, private attributes, setters, other methods
Public attributes, setters, getters, constructor, other methods
Private attributes, constructor, getters, setters, other methods
Other methods, setters, getters, constructor, private attributes
q.why: The reliable pattern is private attributes → constructor → getters → setters → other methods.

q.q: Why is this needed in this.number = number; but not in isLocked = false;?
o: The parameter number has the same name as the attribute; isLocked has no such clash
isLocked is a public attribute, whereas number is a private attribute
this is only needed for int attributes, not for bool attributes
isLocked is set in a method, whereas number is set in the constructor
q.why: this. is used when a parameter shares an attribute's name, to mean this object's attribute.

q.q: When predicting the output of object-oriented code, where are most marks lost according to the notes?
o: Constructors that set attributes from parameters
Conditions inside methods that silently refuse a change
Getters that return an attribute's value unchanged
Calls made with dot notation on each object
q.why: Look for conditions that silently refuse a change, such as ChangeOwner on a locked locker.

q.q: In a class diagram, what does # mean?
o: Public
Private
Protected
Static
q.why: # marks a protected member, visible to the class and its subclasses.

q.q: Which line correctly shows a constructor for class Ticket in a class diagram?
o: + Ticket(price : double) : void
+ Ticket(price : double)
+ GetTicket() : Ticket
- Ticket : double
q.why: A constructor has the class name, its parameters and no return type.

q.q: Which compartment of a class diagram lists - seatsSold : int?
o: The top compartment
The bottom compartment
None; it is not shown
The middle compartment
q.why: Attributes go in the middle compartment; methods go in the bottom one.

q.q: What does the top compartment of a class diagram contain?
o: The attributes
The methods
The subclasses
The class name
q.why: The three compartments are name, attributes and methods.

q.q: What does a minus sign (-) before a member in a class diagram mean?
o: Public: accessible from any code at all
Protected: accessible in the class and its subclasses
Static: shared by every object of the class
Private: accessible only inside the class itself
q.why: + is public, - is private and # is protected.

q.q: Which is the correct class diagram entry for a public method ChangeOwner that takes a string newOwner and returns nothing?
o: - ChangeOwner(newOwner : string) : void
+ ChangeOwner(string) : newOwner
+ ChangeOwner : string(newOwner)
+ ChangeOwner(newOwner : string) : void
q.why: Methods are written as visibility Name(param : type) : returnType.

q.q: In a well-encapsulated class diagram, which symbols would you expect on most attributes and on the public methods?
o: - on attributes and + on methods
+ on attributes and - on methods
# on attributes and - on methods
+ on both attributes and methods
q.why: Attributes are usually private (-) and the methods forming the public interface are public (+).

q.q: A class diagram shows - isbn : string and + GetIsbn() : string but no SetIsbn. What does this show?
o: isbn is a public attribute
isbn can be changed by subclasses
isbn is a read-only attribute
The diagram is missing a method
q.why: A getter with no matching setter shows at a glance that an attribute is read-only.

q.q: Class diagrams are part of which design notation?
o: The Unified Modelling Language (UML)
The data flow diagram notation
Critical path analysis
Structured English pseudocode
q.why: A class diagram is a UML design notation.

q.q: Why are class diagrams drawn before code is written?
o: So the compiler can check the class for errors
So the code runs faster once it is written
So a team can agree what each class will store and do
So that no testing of the class is needed
q.why: They let a team agree the design before coding, then document it for maintainers.

q.q: Item has 2 attributes. Book inherits from Item and adds 2 of its own. How many attributes does a Book object have?
q.why: 2 inherited + 2 of its own = 4.

q.q: Which is another name for a subclass?
o: Derived class
Base class
Parent class
Superclass
q.why: Subclass = derived class = child class; superclass = base class = parent class.

q.q: GetAuthor() is defined only in Book. Book and Dvd both inherit from Item. Can GetAuthor() be called on a Dvd object?
o: No; subclasses do not inherit from each other
Yes, because it is a public method
Yes, because all subclasses share methods
Only if Dvd is declared as abstract
q.why: Dvd inherits only from Item, not from its sibling Book.

q.q: In a class hierarchy diagram, how are the arrowheads drawn?
o: Hollow, pointing up from each subclass to the superclass
Hollow, pointing down from the superclass to each subclass
Filled, pointing up from each subclass to the superclass
Filled, joining each subclass to the other subclasses
q.why: A line from each subclass ends in a hollow arrowhead pointing up to the superclass.

q.q: Which relationship does inheritance model?
o: An 'is a' relationship, such as a book is a library item
A 'has a' relationship, such as a library has books
A 'uses a' relationship, such as a borrower uses a book
A 'calls a' relationship, such as Lend calls Return
q.why: If 'a borrower is a book' sounds wrong, inheritance is the wrong design.

q.q: Item has 2 attributes, Book adds 2, and TextBook inherits from Book and adds 1. How many attributes does a TextBook object have?
q.why: Attributes accumulate down the hierarchy: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

q.q: GetItemId() is defined in Item. Which objects can it be called on?
o: Item objects only
Book and Dvd objects only
Book objects only
Item, Book and Dvd objects
q.why: Methods of the superclass can be used on any subclass object.

q.q: On a class hierarchy diagram, what should the Book box list?
o: Only the members Book adds or overrides
All of Book's members, including inherited ones
Only the members it inherits from Item
Only the methods, not the attributes
q.why: Inherited members are not repeated in a subclass box.

q.q: Which is a complete definition of inheritance?
o: A superclass takes on a subclass's attributes and methods and can add or modify its own
A class hides its attributes and allows access only through get and set methods
A subclass takes on a superclass's attributes and methods and can add or modify its own
Several methods in one class share a name but have different parameter lists
q.why: Both halves are needed: inheriting members, and adding or changing them.

q.q: Which pair of classes is the best candidate for inheritance?
o: Driver as superclass and Bus as subclass
Vehicle as superclass and Bus as subclass
Bus as superclass and Wheel as subclass
Timetable as superclass and Bus as subclass
q.why: A bus is a vehicle, which is an 'is a' relationship; a bus is not a driver, and a wheel is not a bus.

q.q: What does : base(itemId, title) do in the Book constructor?
o: Makes itemId and title public attributes
Passes the values to the superclass constructor
Overrides the Describe method in Item
Declares Book as the superclass of Item
q.why: It calls Item's constructor with those arguments before Book sets its own attribute.

q.q: itemId is private in Item. Inside Book, can you write itemId = "X1";?
o: No; private members cannot be accessed directly by subclass code
Yes, because Book inherits every member
Only inside the Book constructor
Only if Book is declared abstract
q.why: Private members are part of every Book object, but only Item's own code can name them.

q.q: What is printed by Console.WriteLine(bk.LoanDays()); where bk is a Book that does not override LoanDays?
o: It does not compile
q.why: Book does not override LoanDays, so Item's version returns 14.

q.q: How is a subclass Book of Item declared in C#?
o: class Book : Item
class Item : Book
class Book extends Item
class Book inherits Item
q.why: C# uses a colon followed by the base class name.

q.q: title is declared protected in Item. Where can it be used directly?
o: Anywhere in the program
Inside Item and its subclasses only
Inside Item only
Inside subclasses only, not in Item
q.why: Protected members can be used inside subclasses while staying hidden from all other code.

q.q: dv is new Dvd("D044", "Fermanagh From Above", 95). Dvd overrides Describe() to return title + " (DVD, " + GetRuntime() + ")", where GetRuntime() returns minutes + " min". What does dv.Describe() return?
o: D044: Fermanagh From Above
D044: Fermanagh From Above (DVD, 95 min)
Fermanagh From Above (DVD, 95 min)
Fermanagh From Above (DVD, 95)
q.why: Dvd's override replaces Item's version and uses the protected title directly.

q.q: Book overrides Describe() as return base.Describe() + " by " + author;. What does bk.Describe() return for B201, Lough Erne Walks, P. Maguire?
o: Lough Erne Walks by P. Maguire
B201: Lough Erne Walks
B201: Lough Erne Walks by P. Maguire
B201 by P. Maguire
q.why: base.Describe() returns Item's itemId + ": " + title, and Book adds " by " + author.

q.q: What does declaring abstract class Item achieve?
o: Item's attributes all become protected automatically
Every method in Item must be given a body
Subclasses can no longer override Item's methods
new Item(...) will not compile, so every object must be a subclass
q.why: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; it can also declare abstract methods that subclasses must override.

q.q: A subclass constructor leaves out : base(...) and the superclass has no parameterless constructor. What happens?
o: The superclass attributes are set to defaults
A run-time exception is thrown
The code will not compile
The subclass becomes abstract
q.why: The superclass must be initialised, so without a suitable base call the compiler reports an error.

q.q: Inside Dvd, Describe() uses title directly, but Book reaches the ID through base.Describe(). Why?
o: title is private but itemId is protected
title belongs to Dvd but itemId belongs to Book
itemId is public, so it must use a method
title is protected but itemId is private
q.why: Protected members are visible to subclasses; private ones are not, even though they are inherited.

q.q: Which keyword in a base class means subclasses MUST provide their own version of a method?
o: abstract
virtual
override
protected
q.why: An abstract method has no body, so every non-abstract subclass must override it. virtual means they may.

q.q: Two methods in the same class are called Area but take different parameters. This is...
o: overriding
overloading
inheritance
encapsulation
q.why: Same name, different parameter lists, same class: overloading, chosen at compile time.

q.q: When is the overriding version of a method chosen?
o: At compile time, from the variable's declared type
When the programmer writes an if statement
Never; the base version always runs
At run time, from the object's actual class
q.why: Overridden methods are chosen at run time from the actual object's class.

q.q: What is polymorphism?
o: Several methods in one class sharing a name but with different parameters
Objects of different classes responding to the same method call in their own way
A subclass taking on all of the attributes and methods of its superclass
Hiding an object's attributes so they can only be changed through methods
q.why: Polymorphism means 'many forms'; overloading, inheritance and encapsulation are different ideas.

q.q: PitchBooking costs £40 an hour and HallBooking costs £10 plus £25 an hour. Bookings are a 2-hour pitch, a 3-hour hall and a 1.5-hour pitch. What total is output?
If a 1-hour PitchBooking is added to the bookings totalling £225.00, what total is output?
Booking.Summary() calls Cost(). For a HallBooking object, which Cost() runs?
o: Booking's version, because the call is inside Booking
Neither, because Cost is abstract and has no body
PitchBooking's version, as it is listed first
HallBooking's version, chosen from the object's actual class
q.why: Even a call inside the base class runs the subclass's override at run time.

q.q: Which keyword does a subclass use when it replaces a virtual or abstract method?
o: virtual
abstract
override
new
q.why: The base uses virtual or abstract; the subclass uses override.

q.q: A new subclass PoolBooking is added. Why does the foreach loop that calls b.Cost() not need changing?
o: The loop only works with PitchBooking objects
Each object runs its own override, so no type checks are needed
Overloading picks the right method at compile time
PoolBooking inherits PitchBooking's Cost method
q.why: Calling code needs no if statements to test types, so new subclasses fit in easily.

q.q: What does HallBooking's Summary() return for the 3-hour Badminton club booking?
o: Badminton club – £75.00 (incl. £10 set-up)
Badminton club – £85.00
Badminton club – £85.00 (incl. £10 set-up)
Badminton club – £120.00 (incl. £10 set-up)
q.why: Cost is 10 + 3 × 25 = 85, and HallBooking extends base.Summary() with the set-up note.

q.q: Why does OOP reduce the amount of testing needed?
o: Methods inherited from an already-tested superclass need not be retested
Objects never contain errors because their attributes are private
The compiler automatically tests every class when it is built
OOP programs have no loops, so there are fewer paths to test
q.why: Only new or overridden methods in a subclass need fresh testing.

q.q: In which kind of application has OOP been less successful, according to the textbook?
o: Graphical user interfaces
Computer-aided design
Games and simulations
Routine payroll and accounting systems
q.why: OOP has been less successful in routine corporate information systems; it is widely used in CAD, CAM, simulations, games and GUIs.

q.q: Which is a valid disadvantage of OOP?
o: It cannot be used to build graphical user interfaces
It cannot model real-world entities and their behaviour
Very abstract problems do not correspond readily to objects
It has no mechanism for reusing existing code
q.why: Abstract or purely computational problems do not map naturally onto objects.

q.q: How does OOP give more accurate modelling?
o: Classes correspond to real-world entities and their behaviour
Every program becomes a single procedure with no data
Objects use less memory than procedural variables
Classes remove the need to design the system first
q.why: Classes map naturally onto real entities such as patients and wards, making the design easier to discuss with users.

q.q: How does inheritance improve productivity?
o: A superclass automatically has its subclasses' attributes and methods, so less code is written
A subclass automatically has its superclass's attributes and methods, so less new code is written
Every class must be written from scratch, so programmers understand all of the code
Inherited methods run faster than methods written specially for each class
q.why: Reuse through inheritance and class libraries means less new code.

q.q: Why can deep inheritance hierarchies be a disadvantage?
o: They stop subclasses from overriding any methods of the base class
They mean attributes must be declared public in every class
They prevent the program from being compiled into an executable
They are hard to follow, and a fault in a base class spreads to every subclass
q.why: Fragile hierarchies are hard to follow, and changes in a base class affect all subclasses.

q.q: A school needs a 20-line program to calculate the average of a set of marks once. Why might OOP be a poor choice?
o: OOP cannot perform arithmetic such as averages without extra libraries
OOP programs cannot read input from the keyboard or display output
OOP would force the marks to be stored in a database before use
Objects and classes add overhead and design time that is overkill for a small task
q.why: Objects and method calls add memory, processing and design overhead, which is not worth it for small tasks.

q.q: Why is poor class design early in a project a particular risk?
o: Class design can be changed at any time with no effect on other code
Poor class design is always detected automatically by the compiler
Poor class design only affects the speed of the program, not its cost
Identifying classes takes skill and time, and mistakes are costly to fix later
q.why: Complexity and design time are disadvantages: poor early class design is costly to fix later.

q.q: How does encapsulation support teamwork and maintenance in OOP?
o: Every programmer can change any attribute directly, so nobody waits for anyone else
Classes are merged into one large module so that no interfaces need to be agreed
Classes with clear public interfaces can be built separately and changed internally without breaking other code
Public attributes let each team member see and edit the data in every other class
q.why: Self-contained classes with clear interfaces can be built and tested separately.

q.q: What do examiners expect in an 'evaluate the object-oriented approach' answer?
o: A one-word list of advantages, such as reusable and modular, with no conclusion
Developed points on both sides, applied to the scenario, with a justified conclusion
Only the advantages of OOP, since the approach is the modern standard
Only the disadvantages, since evaluation means finding the faults
q.why: Evaluate questions are levels-marked; lists reach only the lowest level.

q.q: In an event-driven program, what determines the order in which code runs?
o: The order the subroutines are written in
The events that occur, such as user actions
The number of controls on the form
The order chosen by the compiler
q.why: Execution order follows events, not a fixed sequence.

q.q: btnSave_Click is an example of...
o: an event
a property
an event handler
a control
q.why: It is the subroutine that runs when the Click event occurs on btnSave.

q.q: Which of these is a property of a TextBox control?
o: Click
Tick
btnOK_Click
Text
q.why: Text holds the contents; Click and Tick are events; btnOK_Click is a handler.

q.q: What is an event?
o: An action or occurrence the program can detect, such as a key press
A subroutine that runs when a button is clicked
An object on a form with properties and methods
The part of the program that waits for input
q.why: The other options describe an event handler, a control and the event loop.

q.q: What does the event loop do?
o: Runs every event handler in turn, in the order written
Waits for events and dispatches each one to its handler
Draws each control on the form when the program starts
Repeats the last event until the user closes the form
q.why: The event loop (started by Application.Run in Windows Forms) waits for events and dispatches them.

q.q: Which is a control?
o: A Button
A click
A key press
An event handler
q.why: Controls are objects on a GUI such as Button, TextBox, Label, CheckBox, ComboBox and Timer.

q.q: The kayak hire handler charges £15 plus £6.50 an hour. The user types 3 and clicks Calculate. What does lblCost show?
o: Kayak hire: £19.50
Kayak hire: £21.50
Kayak hire: £34.50
Kayak hire: £64.50
q.why: 15 + 3 × 6.50 = 34.50, formatted with F2.

q.q: The user leaves the hours box empty and clicks Calculate. Why does the kayak program not crash?
o: int.TryParse returns false, so the else branch shows a message
The empty text is converted to 0 and the cost is £15.00
The Click event is not raised when a text box is empty
Windows Forms ignores any exception in an event handler
q.why: TryParse fails safely and the handler sets lblCost.Text to 'Enter a whole number of hours'.

q.q: Why must event handlers be written to work whatever order events happen in?
o: Users choose what to do next, so events may arrive in any order
The compiler runs handlers in alphabetical order
Each handler runs only once while the program is open
Events are always raised in the order controls were added
q.why: For example, a Save button should be disabled until a file is open, and a text box may still be empty.

q.q: Which shows that event-driven programming and OOP are closely linked?
o: Event handlers cannot be written in procedural languages
Every event handler must be declared as a constructor
A TextBox is an object with properties, methods and events
Controls are created without using any classes
q.why: Controls are objects of classes: a TextBox has properties (Text), methods (Clear) and events (TextChanged).
